notes.meaning: Josiah had already been told that God's judgment on Judah could not be stopped. He did not give up. He did his duty and left the outcome to God, calling all the leaders together so the whole nation could turn back to God with him.

Everyone gathered at the temple, from the greatest to the least, along with priests and prophets. The prophets may have included Jeremiah and Zephaniah. Josiah seems to have read the whole book aloud himself. He did not think it beneath a king to do so, which shows that all people need to know God's Word and leaders should help spread it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars think the book found in the temple was a form of Deuteronomy written not long before Josiah's time. Traditional commentators argue against this idea.

notes.meaning: The pillar was the king's usual place to stand before the people, possibly a raised platform. A covenant is a solemn, binding promise. Here the king renewed the people's promise to follow God with all their heart and keep His laws, and he went first as an example. The people agreed. Many may only have been going through the motions, but the promise still held back a great deal of open wickedness.

Baal and Asherah were false gods of Canaan. "The host of heaven" means the sun, moon and stars. Objects used to worship them were stored in God's own temple, which shows how deep the idol worship ran. Josiah had them burned outside the city, as God's law required. He took the ashes to Bethel to disgrace that place, where Jeroboam had first set up idol worship.

Earlier kings had appointed priests to burn incense at hilltop shrines to Baal, the sun, the moon and the stars. Josiah removed them. Their title may come from the black robes they wore. Real change meant removing the people who led others into sin, not just the objects.

The Asherah pole stood for a false goddess. Manasseh had put it in the temple, later removed it, and his son Amon brought it back. Josiah burned it, ground it to dust and threw the dust on a common graveyard. Graves counted as unclean under God's law, so this showed deep contempt for the idol and for those who had worshipped it.

Sexual sin was practised as part of idol worship, right beside the temple. Women there wove cloth hangings or tents for Asherah worship. Josiah tore it all down. Henry says this was the worst misuse of God's house of all.

High places were hilltop shrines. Many of them were used to worship the true God, but in places He had forbidden. Josiah brought their priests to Jerusalem and spoiled the shrines all over Judah, from Geba in the north to Beersheba in the south. He even tore down the shrines by the city governor's gate, which shows that no one was too important to be corrected.

These priests had worshipped God in the wrong way and place, so they could no longer serve at His altar. They still received food from the priests' share, the way priests with a bodily defect did under the law. It was firm discipline mixed with mercy.

Topheth, in the Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem, was where children were offered to the god Molech. Some were burned, and others were passed through fire to dedicate them. The name may come from the drums beaten to drown out the children's cries. Josiah defiled the place so it could never be used again. This valley later became a picture of hell in the New Testament.

Kings of Judah had given horses to the sun, a custom found among other ancient nations. The horses may have pulled chariots in sun-worship parades, or carried worshippers out to greet the sunrise. Josiah took the horses away and burned the chariots.

People built altars on flat rooftops to worship the stars. Manasseh had set up altars in the temple courts and removed them after he repented, but his son Amon seems to have brought them back. Josiah smashed them all and threw the dust into the Kidron Valley, to wipe out even the memory of them.

The "Mount of Corruption" was part of the Mount of Olives, nicknamed for the idol worship there. Solomon had built shrines there for foreign gods, and the site was still treated as holy centuries later. Josiah defiled it. False worship, once started, can last far longer than anyone expects.

Josiah smashed the stone pillars and cut down the poles used in idol worship. He then filled those places with human bones, the worst defilement possible under the law. This made the old worship sites disgusting, so no one would want to go back.

Jeroboam, the first king of northern Israel, had set up an altar at Bethel to keep his people from worshipping in Jerusalem. The northern kingdom was now gone, and Josiah's reform reached into that land. The golden calf seems to have been gone, but the altar still stood. Josiah tore it down, burned it and ground it to powder.

Josiah noticed tombs nearby, perhaps of the idol priests, and burned their bones on the altar to defile it. This is exactly what a man of God had foretold about 300 years earlier, even naming Josiah (1 Kings 13:2). It looked like a sudden decision, yet God had said it long before. His word never fails.

A marker showed the grave of the prophet who had foretold all this, and Josiah ordered it left alone. The old prophet from Samaria, who had once deceived him, was buried in the same grave, so his bones were spared too. Henry notes that God's displeasure with the man of God ended at his death, and here God honoured his memory.

Josiah carried his reform into the towns of the old northern kingdom too. He seems to have seen himself as king over all of God's people, and many Israelites left in the land welcomed it. As Henry puts it, our efforts to do good should reach as far as our influence goes.

These priests had led people into idol worship, and under God's law their lives were forfeit. Josiah put them to death on their own altars and burned bones there, as the old prophecy had said. Then he went home to Jerusalem.

Passover is the yearly feast remembering how God rescued Israel from Egypt. After clearing away evil, Josiah turned to doing good. He commanded the people to keep the feast just as the newly found book said. Neglecting it had shown that the people had forgotten how God saved them.

There had been earlier Passovers, but none kept so carefully by the rules of God's law since Samuel's day. People from both Judah and the old northern kingdom took part, with great zeal and preparation. It was a time of deep, holy joy, and it came in the same year the book was found.

Mediums and spiritists were people who claimed to contact the dead or spirits. Household gods were small idols kept at home. Josiah removed all of them, even those people tried to hide. In everything he did, the book of God's law was his guide.

These words echo the great command to love God with all your heart, soul and strength (Deuteronomy 6:5). Hezekiah stood out for trusting God in hard times. Josiah stood out for wholehearted zeal in bringing people back to God's ways. His faith was real "heart-work," and he followed God's law carefully. Clarke says David was a greater man, but not a better one.

Even after all this, God's judgment stood. The people had obeyed the king outwardly, but their hearts had not truly turned. The prophets Jeremiah and Zephaniah show they still loved their idols. Because of Josiah, the judgment was put off during his lifetime, but not cancelled.

God had decided that Judah would be sent away just as Israel had been. Even Jerusalem and the temple would be rejected. His promises to the city depended on the people staying faithful, and they had not. Henry adds that even this judgment was meant, in the end, to cure them of their sin.
The writer points readers to another record for the rest of Josiah's story. Second Chronicles 35 also gives a fuller account of his Passover and his death.

Pharaoh Neco of Egypt was marching north to the Euphrates River, and Josiah went out to stop him. He may have feared what Egypt would do to his land. But he had no clear call from God to fight, and he did not ask God's will. He was killed at Megiddo. Many see his death as a rebuke for this rashness, yet also as a mercy: he died at peace with God and did not live to see Jerusalem fall.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Kings and Chronicles preserve two different accounts. Kings may describe Josiah being killed at a meeting with Neco, while Chronicles says he was wounded in battle.

notes.meaning: Josiah was badly wounded and carried to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried (2 Chronicles 35:24). His loss was a mercy to him but a blow to his people, for it opened the door to their ruin. The people chose his younger son Jehoahaz as king, perhaps because he seemed bolder and more warlike.
Jehoahaz was younger than his brother Eliakim, but the people put him on the throne. Jeremiah calls him Shallum. He ruled only three months.

Even with a godly father and a good upbringing, Jehoahaz followed wicked kings like Manasseh and Amon and brought back idol worship. Ezekiel pictures him as a young lion that learned to devour people. It matters a great deal whose example we choose to follow.
Neco put Jehoahaz in chains at Riblah in Syria. He had taken the throne without Egypt's approval. Neco also forced Judah to pay a heavy tribute, a payment made to show it was under his rule.

Neco put Josiah's older son Eliakim on the throne and gave him a new name, Jehoiakim, meaning "the LORD will raise up." Renaming him showed that Pharaoh was now his master, though the new name still honoured Israel's God. Jehoahaz was taken to Egypt and died there.

Jehoiakim paid Pharaoh by taxing his people according to their wealth. Clarke fears this bad king did not keep even that rule fairly. Henry notes the sad reversal: Israel once took Egypt's riches when they left, and now Egypt was taking theirs. This is what sin brings.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five and ruled eleven years. His mother came from Rumah, a town not mentioned anywhere else, which may be Aruma near Shechem.

Hard times did not make Jehoiakim good. Jeremiah describes him as a greedy tyrant who oppressed his people, and he even killed the prophet Urijah. Josiah honoured God's Word, but his son later burned it. Yet the good work God begins in a heart by His Spirit cannot be undone.
